title: Timing heuristics
examples: How should I pace myself during the exam?
What is a good rule of thumb for different mark types?
Can I estimate how long I have for a whole paper?

explain.say: Today we learn about timing heuristics for exams.
A marks per minute guide helps you plan your writing time.
For a simple recall question worth two marks, you might spend two minutes.
If a question is worth six marks, aim to spend about six minutes writing your answer.
For a longer question worth twelve marks, you should plan for around twelve minutes.
When doing a real exam, look at the total marks and divide by the total time.

faq.q: Does this guide work for every subject?
faq.a: It is a general guideline, not a strict rule for every single paper. You must adjust it based on the question type.
asks: Is this rule for science too?
Does the subject matter change the timing?

faq.q: What if a question is very difficult to answer?
faq.a: If you get stuck, spend a short time, make a note, and move on. You can return to it later if time allows.
asks: Should I spend all my time on one hard question?
What if I don't know the answer?

faq.q: Should I spend more time on questions worth more marks?
faq.a: Yes, generally you should spend proportionally more time on questions that carry more marks. This is the core idea of pacing.
asks: Is it okay to rush the big questions?
How do I prioritize my time?

faq.q: Can I use this guide if I am writing an essay?
faq.a: For essays, think of the marks as being spread across your introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Allocate time to each section.
asks: Does this apply to long written answers?
How do I pace an essay?

faq.q: What if the exam paper is very long?
faq.a: If the paper is very long, first calculate the average marks per minute across the whole paper to set a baseline pace.
asks: What if there are many questions?
How do I start my timing plan?

facts: Pacing heuristics help students manage their time during exams.
The guide suggests allocating time based on the marks awarded for a question.
If a question is worth six marks, aiming for about six minutes is a starting point.
Students should always use this guide as a flexible tool, not a rigid law.

quiz.say: If you have a total of 20 marks in 40 minutes, what is your ideal pace?
quiz.why: You divide the total marks by the total time to find your average required pace.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the total marks by the total time.
wrong.1: This reverses the calculation, suggesting you have too much time.
wrong.3: This suggests you are working twice as fast as you should be.

quiz.say: For a very detailed, high-mark question, which approach is best?

options.show: Spend the least time on the hardest questions.
options.say: Spend the least time on the hardest questions.

options.show: Spend time based only on how long it takes you.
options.say: Spend time based only on how long it takes you.

options.show: Allocate time proportional to the marks awarded.
options.say: Allocate time proportional to the marks awarded.

options.show: Spend the same time on every question.
options.say: Spend the same time on every question.

quiz.why: The goal is to spend more time on areas that carry more marks to achieve a higher score.

wrong.0: You must dedicate sufficient time to complex questions to fully answer them.
wrong.1: Your personal speed is less important than the marks the examiner is awarding.
wrong.3: This ignores the marking scheme and will leave you unprepared for high-value questions.
